name: Roll from Dead Orchard
description: A Dead Orchard reset opens the high both-arm leg triangle before turning or reorganizing guard. A rolling headlock escape needs a separate starting position.
summary: A Dead Orchard reset releases the high both-arm leg triangle before the bottom player turns or reorganizes guard.
overview:
The bottom player is already facing the opponent in Dead Orchard Control, with a high rubber-guard leg connection. Dead Orchard is not an Anaconda front headlock. A rolling headlock escape cannot be taught from this configuration without a separate headlock exchange.

The bottom player faces the opponent and keeps the hips close beneath the shoulders. The legs form a high figure-four around the shoulder line, with both opposing arms inside. Release any wrist, neck or elbow loading before opening the high-leg enclosure. Lower the controlling leg through a comfortable hip angle rather than pulling the foot against the knee.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Nathan Orchard — Dead Orchard, part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoiB1D2WJwE); [Ben Eddy — the Zombie pummel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JzSxFvNA5Uo).

defender.name: Roll from Dead Orchard Defender
defender.description: Roll from Dead Orchard (defender): Treat a high leg triangle containing both your arms as an arm-lock threat even when the neck is not being choked. Keep the arms compact and avoid offering a straight arm while trying to force posture.
defender.overview:
The bottom player is already facing the opponent in Dead Orchard Control, with a high rubber-guard leg connection. Dead Orchard is not an Anaconda front headlock. A rolling headlock escape cannot be taught from this configuration without a separate headlock exchange.

Treat a high leg triangle containing both your arms as an arm-lock threat even when the neck is not being choked. Keep the arms compact and avoid offering a straight arm while trying to force posture. Maintain an early frame at the hip or thigh before the figure-four closes around the shoulders.

Work on opening the leg enclosure before withdrawing the shoulder and elbow together; stop if an arm is already loaded. Only raise posture after the shoulder line is free; a sudden pull can extend a captured elbow. Use a verbal tap or foot tap if both hands are trapped, and do not rely on pain to judge remaining range.
